concept.name: Multi-Region Disaster Recovery

relationships.description: Connects Multi-Region Disaster Recovery to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Multi-region disaster recovery (DR) protects workloads against a total regional cloud outage by replicating data to a secondary region and maintaining a tested recovery path—ranging from cheap Backup & Restore to Warm Standby—sized strictly to your RPO (acceptable data loss) and RTO (acceptable downtime).
spark.keyTakeaway: Disaster recovery is an SLA-driven economics exercise: you pay exponentially more as RPO and RTO shrink toward zero, and an untested DR runbook is indistinguishable from having no DR at all.

concept.whyItMatters: Even if a single cloud region spans 3+ Availability Zones, correlated failures—bad control-plane pushes, regional fiber cuts, DNS/IAM outages, or ransomware—can take an entire region offline for hours. Defining explicit RPO/RTO targets and automating cross-region recovery prevents existential data loss and multi-hour revenue blackouts without paying 2x+ for full active-active.
whenToUse: Regulatory, contractual, or business SLAs require surviving a full regional outage, but 5–60 minutes of failover time (RTO) is acceptable.
Cost constraints make running 2x active-active compute prohibitive, so a scaled-down standby or automated IaC rebuild fits the budget.
Workloads have clear primary-writer semantics (e.g., an ERP, billing ledger, or internal platform) where avoiding multi-master write conflicts is critical.
whenNotToUse: The business requires zero-second failover (RTO < 30s) and zero data loss (RPO = 0) across regions—that requires Multi-Region Active-Active.
The application already runs statelessly on an edge/global platform where losing a region only shifts traffic without stateful recovery.
You haven't first implemented multi-AZ high availability inside your primary region—multi-AZ solves 99% of hardware/power failures much more cheaply.
keyPoints: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) dictates your replication technology: async WAL/snapshot shipping gives minutes of RPO, while Aurora Global Database or synchronous storage replication achieves <1–5 seconds.
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) dictates how much pre-warmed compute you pay for: Backup & Restore takes hours, Pilot Light takes 10–30 minutes, and Warm Standby takes 1–5 minutes.
DNS TTLs and Route 53 health checks are often the slowest part of failover—use low TTLs (30–60s) or Global Accelerator/Anycast endpoints.
Fencing against split-brain is mandatory: when promoting Region B, revoke Region A's write credentials or fence its primary DB so a recovering Region A cannot accept stale writes.
Unverified backups are worthless; automate monthly GameDays (using AWS FIS or Terraform + Chaos scripts) to measure actual end-to-end RTO.

examples.title: Fintech Ledger on Pilot Light DR
examples.scenario: A B2B payments platform runs PostgreSQL on AWS `us-east-1` with Aurora Global Database streaming redo logs to `us-west-2` (<1s lag). In `us-west-2`, only the DB replica and core VPC/IAM/KMS infrastructure run continuously; ECS/EKS compute scales from 0 via Terraform on failover.
examples.outcome: Standby spend stays under 18% of primary cost while achieving an RPO of <2 seconds and a tested RTO of 12 minutes.

examples.title: SaaS Control Plane on Warm Standby
examples.scenario: An enterprise workflow SaaS runs 100% traffic in `eu-west-1` and keeps a 20%-sized Warm Standby cluster active in `eu-central-1` receiving synthetic canary traffic every 60 seconds.
examples.outcome: During a `eu-west-1` networking brownout, Route 53 health checks fail over in 60 seconds and autoscaling expands `eu-central-1` to 100% capacity in 4 minutes.

tradeOffs.factor: DR Tier (Backup & Restore vs. Pilot Light vs. Warm Standby)
tradeOffs.pro: Backup & Restore costs almost nothing beyond S3 cross-region storage (~5% overhead).
tradeOffs.con: Rebuilding VPCs, clusters, and restoring multi-terabyte DB snapshots from cold storage can take 4–12 hours (high RTO).

tradeOffs.pro: Asynchronous replication adds zero latency to primary-region user writes.
tradeOffs.con: In a sudden regional power/network blackout, the last few seconds of committed transactions in flight are lost (RPO > 0).

tradeOffs.pro: Automated failover cuts RTO from 30 minutes of human pager response to <2 minutes.
tradeOffs.con: False-positive health checks can trigger an unnecessary failover, causing split-brain or brief data loss if not tightly gated.

failureModes.name: Cold-Start Capacity & Quota Exhaustion
failureModes.description: During a major AWS/GCP regional outage, thousands of customers fail over to `us-west-2` simultaneously; Pilot Light fails because the secondary region lacks EC2/GPU quota or spot capacity.
failureModes.mitigation: Pre-request matching vCPU/DB service quotas in the DR region and reserve Capacity Reservations for critical core nodes.

failureModes.name: Stale IaC & Configuration Drift
failureModes.description: Engineers add environment variables, IAM roles, or security group rules in the primary region over 6 months without updating the DR Terraform workspace, causing failover boot crashes.
failureModes.mitigation: Deploy identical Terraform/Helm modules to both regions via CI/CD on every merge; validate DR config daily with synthetic health checks.

failureModes.name: Ransomware / Logical Corruption Replication
failureModes.description: An accidental `DROP TABLE` or ransomware encryption in Region A replicates faithfully to Region B's warm replica within 1 second, destroying both copies.
failureModes.mitigation: Pair real-time replication with immutable, air-gapped backups (S3 Object Lock in Compliance Mode) in a separate AWS/GCP security account.

failureModes.name: Failback Data Divergence
failureModes.description: After failing over to Region B for 3 hours, engineers hastily switch DNS back to Region A without re-syncing the 3 hours of new writes made in Region B.
failureModes.mitigation: Treat failback as a planned reverse-DR migration: reverse replication from B -> A, verify checksums, drain traffic, and cut over cleanly.

commonMistakes: Storing DR runbooks and Terraform state only inside the primary region (e.g., an S3 bucket in `us-east-1` that is unreachable during the outage).
Using the same KMS key or Secrets Manager region across both deployments, leaving the DR cluster unable to decrypt database backups.
Confusing backups with DR: taking nightly RDS snapshots without testing `pg_restore` time on a 4TB database.
Forgetting third-party webhook allowlists—Stripe, Okta, or bank APIs reject requests from the DR region's NAT Gateway IPs because they weren't pre-allowlisted.
Triggering automated failover on a single noisy health check instead of requiring multi-POP consensus.

sections.content:
## The idea

Multi-region disaster recovery (DR) is an **active-passive** resilience strategy. One primary region serves 100% of production traffic during normal operations while a secondary DR region stays ready to take over if the primary becomes unusable.

Unlike active-active, DR avoids multi-master write conflicts and keeps baseline compute costs low. The architecture is governed by two hard contracts: **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)**—the maximum tolerable age of lost data—and **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)**—the maximum tolerable downtime from outage detection to restored service. Every design decision maps directly to those two numbers.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through a **Pilot Light** failover for a financial SaaS running in `us-east-1` (Primary) and `us-west-2` (DR):

1. **Steady-State Replication**: Primary Aurora PostgreSQL in `us-east-1` streams redo logs continuously to a headless read replica in `us-west-2` (~800ms lag). S3 buckets replicate encrypted objects via Cross-Region Replication (CRR) with Object Lock.
2. **Failure Detection**: Route 53 health checks from 15+ global edge locations fail 3 consecutive `/healthz` probes (45 seconds) against `us-east-1`.
3. **Fencing & Promotion**: An automated Step Function / Runbook in `us-west-2` fences `us-east-1` (revokes primary write IAM/SG ingress) and promotes the `us-west-2` Aurora replica to standalone primary writer (~45 seconds).
4. **Compute Scale-Out**: Terraform/ArgoCD scales `us-west-2` EKS node groups and application pods from 0 to production replicas using pre-replicated ECR container images (~4 minutes).
5. **Traffic Cutover**: Route 53 updates weighted DNS records (60s TTL) to point `api.saas.com` to `us-west-2` ALB, restoring service in ~7 minutes total.

sections.content:
## Choosing the right DR tier

Cloud DR architectures fall into four standard tiers ordered by increasing cost and decreasing RTO:

1. **Backup & Restore**: Periodic snapshots + IaC templates replicated cross-region. Cheapest (~5% extra cost), but slow (hours).
2. **Pilot Light**: Core data stores replicate live in the DR region while compute stays off (0 replicas). Moderate cost (~15–20%), RTO 10–30 minutes.
3. **Warm Standby**: A scaled-down (e.g., 10–25%) full stack runs continuously in the DR region, verified by synthetic tests. Higher cost (~30–50%), RTO 1–5 minutes.
4. **Multi-Site Active-Active**: Full capacity in all regions; effectively RTO ~0s at 2x+ cost.

## DR tier comparison

| DR Strategy | Typical RPO | Typical RTO | Standby Compute | Best For | Primary Operational Risk |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Backup & Restore** | 1–24 hours | 4–12 hours | None | Internal tools, batch analytics, dev/staging | Snapshot restore speed on multi-TB DBs |
| **Pilot Light** | Seconds–5 min | 10–30 min | DB replica only | Core SaaS, B2B APIs, financial ledgers | Cold-start quota limits or drifted IaC |
| **Warm Standby** | Seconds | 1–5 min | Scaled-down (10–25%) | Customer-facing apps with tight SLAs | Autoscaling lag during sudden 4x surge |
| **Active-Active** | 0–Seconds | <15 sec | 100% live everywhere | Global Tier-0 payments, auth, edge APIs | Write conflicts & cross-region egress |

## Failure modes

The most common DR failure is **corrupt or unreachable control-plane dependencies**. If your CI/CD runner, Terraform state bucket, or KMS encryption keys live exclusively in `us-east-1`, you cannot execute your `us-west-2` failover runbook when `us-east-1` is down. Always host failover automation and state in the DR region (or a third neutral region).

Second, beware **failover oscillation and split-brain**: if `us-east-1` flaps up and down due to packet loss, automated failover can leave half the clients writing to `us-west-2` and half to `us-east-1`. Require manual human confirmation for full regional promotion unless your fencing mechanism is 100% deterministic.

## GameDays and continuous verification

A DR plan decays within weeks of being written due to schema changes, new secrets, and third-party IP allowlists. Run **quarterly live GameDays** (or monthly for Warm Standby) where you actually fail over staging—or a canary slice of production—to the DR region, measure real RPO/RTO with a stopwatch, and execute the full **failback** procedure.

Pair live drills with daily automated **DR readiness checks**: verify replication lag < threshold, ECR image parity, KMS key availability, and service quota headroom in the DR region.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] **Quantify RPO & RTO**: Get written sign-off from product/compliance before choosing Pilot Light vs. Warm Standby.
- [ ] **Decouple DR control plane**: Store Terraform state, runbooks, and container registries in the DR region too.
- [ ] **Pre-approve quotas & IPs**: Request matching vCPU/DB quotas and allowlist DR NAT Gateway IPs with external partners.
- [ ] **Replicate secrets & KMS**: Enable multi-region KMS keys or independent encryption pipelines for DR backups.
- [ ] **Protect against corruption**: Combine real-time replication with immutable, air-gapped backups (Object Lock) in a separate account.
- [ ] **Test failback too**: Document and rehearse how to re-sync new DR writes back to the primary region after recovery.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Multi Region Disaster Recovery

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Multi-region disaster recovery (DR) protects workloads against a total regional cloud outage by replicating data to a secondary region and maintaining a tested recovery path—ranging from cheap Backup & Restore to Warm Standby—sized strictly to your RPO (acceptable data loss) and RTO (acceptable downtime).

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: DR Data Replica applies the primary invariant and coordinates with DR Standby Compute.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, DR Standby Compute experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Pre-request matching vCPU/DB service quotas in the DR region and reserve Capacity Reservations for critical core nodes.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Disaster recovery is an SLA-driven economics exercise: you pay exponentially more as RPO and RTO shrink toward zero, and an untested DR runbook is indistinguishable from having no DR at all.
Avoid trap: Storing DR runbooks and Terraform state only inside the primary region (e.g., an S3 bucket in `us-east-1` that is unreachable during the outage).
Avoid trap: Using the same KMS key or Secrets Manager region across both deployments, leaving the DR cluster unable to decrypt database backups.
When to reach for it: Regulatory, contractual, or business SLAs require surviving a full regional outage, but 5–60 minutes of failover time (RTO) is acceptable.
When to reach for it: Cost constraints make running 2x active-active compute prohibitive, so a scaled-down standby or automated IaC rebuild fits the budget.

putItTogether.title: Putting Multi Region Disaster Recovery Together
putItTogether.summary: Disaster recovery is an SLA-driven economics exercise: you pay exponentially more as RPO and RTO shrink toward zero, and an untested DR runbook is indistinguishable from having no DR at all.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Multi Region Disaster Recovery before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Standby spend stays under 18% of primary cost while achieving an RPO of <2 seconds and a tested RTO of 12 minutes.
